overview:
By the eight centuries covered here, the word had already stopped meaning the same thing everywhere. "Neolithic" names a way of living — farming, herding, permanent settlement, polished stone tools, pottery — rather than a slice of time, and because agriculture was taken up at wildly different dates in different places, the period begins and ends region by region. In the Near East, where domestication started around 9000 BCE, the Neolithic was long over by 3000 BCE: southern Mesopotamia had walled cities, temple bureaucracies and the first writing, and Egypt had been unified under a single king. What the label covers in this window is everything happening outside those early literate cores, which was most of the inhabited world.

In Europe the third millennium is the Late Neolithic proper, and it was turbulent. The middle Neolithic pattern of large settlements and collective tombs — the long tradition of megalithic building that raised passage graves, stone rows and, in Britain, the sarsen circle at Stonehenge — gave way after roughly 2800 BCE to the Corded Ware complex, a strikingly uniform spread of single graves with cord-impressed pots and stone battle-axes running from the Rhine to the Volga. Ancient DNA published since 2015 has tied that shift to large-scale migration from the Pontic-Caspian steppe, and it is now argued to be the main vector by which Indo-European languages entered Europe, though how much of the change was migration, how much emulation, and how violent the process was remain genuinely disputed. Overlapping it came the Bell Beaker network and, at the far end of the window, the first regular use of copper and then tin bronze, which is what conventionally closes the Neolithic. Underneath the burials sits a quieter revolution: the broadening use of animals for milk, wool, traction and transport, with ard ploughs, ox-carts and wheels appearing across the continent early in the millennium.

Elsewhere the same centuries carried their own late-Neolithic worlds. In the Yellow River valley the Longshan culture, roughly 3000 to 1900 BCE, built dozens of rammed-earth walled towns — Taosi enclosed nearly three square kilometres — produced eggshell-thin black pottery on the wheel, and left tombs stratified enough to imply hereditary rank, laying the ground for the Bronze Age kingdoms that followed. In highland New Guinea, where taro and banana cultivation was already thousands of years old, villages, ground stone tools and ritual objects become archaeologically visible around 3000 to 2200 BCE, apparently without outside prompting. In Mesoamerica and the Andes, farming villages based on maize, squash, beans and tubers were spreading toward the density they would reach by 2000 BCE. None of these societies had metal in daily use, and none of them wrote; they are known almost entirely from what they buried and abandoned.
significance: This is the last stretch in which most of humanity lived beyond the reach of any state or script, and it is also where the demographic and social foundations of nearly everything after were laid: heritable property in land and animals, ranked burial, fortified towns, wheeled transport and traction, and populations large enough to sustain full-time specialists. In Europe the third-millennium reshuffling left a genetic and probably linguistic signature that most of the continent still carries. In China the Longshan walled towns are the direct ancestors of Shang urbanism. And because the Neolithic ends at different dates in different places — around 2000 BCE in northern Europe, much later in parts of Africa, the Pacific and the Americas — the period is a standing reminder that world history has no single clock, and that the societies without cities or archives in any given century were not behind so much as elsewhere.
coverage: Written from general reference works and summaries of the archaeological and ancient-DNA literature; the dataset itself holds no events under this story, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped place or date. The underlying record is entirely material — graves, pots, post-holes, pollen and genomes — with no written testimony from any of these societies, so motives, languages, kinship and belief are inference rather than evidence; the scale and character of the steppe migration into Europe, and whether Corded Ware uniformity reflects population replacement or adopted fashion, are actively contested. Coverage is also badly uneven: temperate Europe and north China are intensively excavated, while Africa south of the Sahara, interior South America and much of Southeast Asia in these centuries are thinly sampled.
